name: population parameter versus sample statistic
essential_semantics: A population quantity (fixed, unknown) and a sample quantity (random, computed from data) are distinct objects with distinct types.
canonical_example: mu versus xbar
rationale: Every inferential error of the 'the mean is 5' kind stems from collapsing these; the distinction is the foundation of statistics.

name: dataset with declared structure
essential_semantics: An indexed collection of observations with unit of observation, variable names and per-variable measurement types.
canonical_example: n observations of (y_i, x_i) for i = 1..n
rationale: The unit of observation determines independence structure; an untyped table cannot express it.

name: measurement scale of a variable
essential_semantics: Nominal, ordinal, interval and ratio scales determine which operations are meaningful (means of ordinals, ratios of interval data).
canonical_example: temperature in Celsius is interval, so ratios are meaningless
rationale: Stevens' scale typing is a genuine constraint on admissible operations that numeric typing alone does not capture.

name: observed versus latent quantity
essential_semantics: Which variables are observed and which are unobserved is part of the model, determining the likelihood and the inference target.
canonical_example: z_i latent class, y_i observed response
rationale: Latency drives marginalisation; a model that does not mark observability cannot derive its own likelihood.

name: estimator as a function of data
essential_semantics: A rule mapping a dataset to a value, itself a random variable via the data; distinct from the estimate it produces.
canonical_example: the estimator Xbar_n versus the estimate 4.2
rationale: Sampling distributions are the pushforward of the data law under the estimator; without estimators as functions there is no sampling distribution.

name: sampling distribution of a statistic
essential_semantics: The law of an estimator under repeated sampling, dependent on the assumed data-generating process.
canonical_example: under normality, Xbar ~ Normal(mu, sigma^2/n)
rationale: Frequentist guarantees are statements about this distribution; if it cannot be named, the guarantees cannot be stated.

name: bias of an estimator
essential_semantics: E[estimator] - target, relative to a specified data-generating distribution.
canonical_example: the MLE of variance is biased downward by a factor (n-1)/n
rationale: Bias is defined only relative to an assumed truth; representations that omit the assumed model make it meaningless.

name: consistency
essential_semantics: Convergence of an estimator to the target as sample size grows, in a stated mode.
canonical_example: thetahat_n -> theta in probability
rationale: An asymptotic property that is meaningless without the mode of convergence and the sequence structure.

name: efficiency, variance and MSE of an estimator
essential_semantics: Risk decomposition into bias and variance under a stated loss, and comparison against a bound.
canonical_example: MSE = bias^2 + variance; Cramer-Rao lower bound
rationale: Comparing estimators requires a loss function to be stated, not implied.

name: sufficient statistic
essential_semantics: A statistic carrying all information about a parameter, defined by conditional independence of the data from the parameter given the statistic.
canonical_example: sum of x_i is sufficient for the Poisson rate
rationale: A clean example of a statistical concept that is exactly a conditional-independence statement.

name: Fisher information
essential_semantics: Expected negative Hessian of the log-likelihood with respect to the parameter, a matrix-valued function of the parameter.
canonical_example: I(theta) = -E[d^2/dtheta^2 log L(theta; X)]
rationale: It composes differentiation, expectation and matrix structure in one object, a useful stress test.

name: likelihood as a function of the parameter
essential_semantics: The same formula as the density but with data fixed and parameter varying; a likelihood is not a probability distribution over parameters.
canonical_example: L(theta; x) = p(x | theta) viewed as a function of theta
rationale: The role reversal of arguments is the defining move of inference and is exactly the kind of fact a representation loses if it stores only a formula.

name: log-likelihood and additivity over independent observations
essential_semantics: Sum over observations of log densities, valid only under an independence assumption that must be recorded.
canonical_example: l(theta) = sum_i log p(x_i | theta)
rationale: The additive form encodes an independence assumption; writing it without that assumption is a hidden modelling claim.

name: maximum likelihood estimation
essential_semantics: Argmax over a declared parameter space of the likelihood, with existence and uniqueness not assumed.
canonical_example: thetahat = argmax_{theta in Theta} L(theta; x)
rationale: It is the canonical composition of statistics with optimisation, including a constrained parameter space.

name: prior distribution over parameters
essential_semantics: A distribution over the parameter space, requiring parameters to be typed as random variables, with propriety declared.
canonical_example: theta ~ Beta(2, 2)
rationale: Treating a parameter as random is a substantive commitment; improper priors additionally require a propriety check on the posterior.

name: posterior distribution
essential_semantics: The conditional distribution of parameters given data, distinct from the likelihood and from a point estimate.
canonical_example: p(theta | x)
rationale: The four-way distinction prior/likelihood/posterior/predictive is a hard test of distributional typing.

name: predictive distribution
essential_semantics: Distribution over new observations obtained by integrating the likelihood over the posterior.
canonical_example: p(xnew | x) = integral p(xnew | theta) p(theta | x) dtheta
rationale: It requires integrating a distribution-valued function over another distribution, a genuinely higher-order construction.

name: credible interval
essential_semantics: An interval carrying posterior probability mass, a statement about the parameter given the data.
canonical_example: P(theta in [a,b] | x) = 0.95
rationale: Its interpretation differs fundamentally from a confidence interval; keeping them distinct is a real semantic requirement.

name: confidence interval
essential_semantics: A random interval whose coverage probability is a property of the procedure, not of a particular realised interval.
canonical_example: P(theta in [L(X), U(X)]) = 0.95 over repeated sampling
rationale: The coverage statement quantifies over the random interval, not the parameter; systems that store only endpoints lose the quantifier structure entirely.

name: null and alternative hypotheses
essential_semantics: Two disjoint subsets of the parameter space, with simple versus composite hypotheses distinguished.
canonical_example: H0: mu = 0 versus H1: mu != 0
rationale: A hypothesis is a set of parameter values; representing it as a number makes composite hypotheses inexpressible.

name: test statistic and its null distribution
essential_semantics: A statistic together with its distribution under the null hypothesis, including whether that distribution is exact or asymptotic.
canonical_example: t = (xbar - mu0)/(s/sqrt(n)) ~ t_{n-1} under H0
rationale: The exact/asymptotic status of a null distribution is a validity condition that is routinely omitted.

name: p-value
essential_semantics: Probability, under the null, of a test statistic at least as extreme as observed; a conditional probability of data given hypothesis, never of hypothesis given data.
canonical_example: p = P(T >= t_obs | H0)
rationale: The direction of conditioning is the most misinterpreted fact in applied statistics; a faithful representation must fix it.

name: type I and type II error rates
essential_semantics: Error probabilities under the null and under a specified alternative respectively, both conditional and both procedure-level.
canonical_example: alpha = 0.05, beta depends on the true effect size
rationale: Type II error is defined only relative to an alternative, a dependency frequently left implicit.

name: statistical power as a function of the alternative
essential_semantics: A function from the alternative parameter value to detection probability, not a single number.
canonical_example: power(delta) = P(reject H0 | mu = delta)
rationale: Reporting 'power = 0.8' without the effect size is an incomplete statement, which a typed representation would catch.

name: multiplicity and error-rate control
essential_semantics: The number of tests performed and the family-wise or false-discovery criterion are part of the inferential claim.
canonical_example: Bonferroni adjustment across m tests
rationale: The family of tests is context that changes the meaning of each p-value; representing tests in isolation hides it.

name: effect size distinguished from significance
essential_semantics: A magnitude, typically with units or standardisation, separate from the evidence measure against a null.
canonical_example: a difference of 0.3 kg with p = 0.001
rationale: Magnitude and evidence are different quantities; conflating them is one of the field's standard failures.

name: linear model with explicit error structure
essential_semantics: y = X beta + epsilon with the distribution of epsilon, the shape of X and the conditioning on X all stated.
canonical_example: y_i = beta_0 + beta_1 x_i + eps_i, eps_i iid Normal(0, sigma^2)
rationale: It is the most common applied model and simultaneously exercises shape typing, indexing and distributional assumptions.

name: design matrix and encoding of covariates
essential_semantics: Mapping from variables (including categorical ones) to columns, with the contrast/encoding scheme explicit.
canonical_example: a 3-level factor becomes 2 dummy columns under treatment coding
rationale: Coefficient interpretation depends entirely on the encoding, which is usually implicit and therefore lost.

name: generalised linear model with link and family
essential_semantics: A response family, a link function and a linear predictor as three separately identified components.
canonical_example: logit(E[Y|x]) = x^T beta with Y ~ Bernoulli
rationale: The link acts on the mean, not on the response; representations that apply it to the data are wrong.

name: random effects and grouped structure
essential_semantics: Parameters that are themselves random, indexed by group, with a covariance structure over groups.
canonical_example: y_ij = beta + u_j + eps_ij, u_j ~ Normal(0, tau^2)
rationale: Nested indexing plus random parameters is where flat modelling languages break down.

name: residual versus error
essential_semantics: The unobservable error term and the computed residual are different objects with different distributions.
canonical_example: eps_i is unobserved; e_i = y_i - yhat_i is computed
rationale: Diagnostics rely on knowing that residuals are not the errors; the distinction is silently dropped in most notation.

name: model comparison criteria
essential_semantics: Criteria such as AIC, BIC, WAIC with their assumptions and the comparability conditions (same data, same response scale).
canonical_example: AIC = -2 log L + 2k
rationale: Comparability preconditions are exactly the sort of side condition a faithful representation should carry.

name: resampling-based evaluation
essential_semantics: A partitioning scheme respecting the dependence structure of the data, with the scheme itself part of the reported result.
canonical_example: 5-fold CV grouped by subject to avoid leakage
rationale: Leakage is a dependence-structure violation; representing the scheme makes it checkable.

name: bootstrap and resampling distributions
essential_semantics: Approximating a sampling distribution by resampling, with the approximation status explicit.
canonical_example: bootstrap percentile interval for the median
rationale: The resulting interval is doubly approximate (resampling plus Monte Carlo error), which should be recorded.

name: Markov chain Monte Carlo inference
essential_semantics: Approximating a posterior by a chain with a declared target, whose output is correlated samples, not exact draws.
canonical_example: Hamiltonian Monte Carlo targeting p(theta | x)
rationale: Convergence and autocorrelation qualifications are part of the inferential claim, not implementation trivia.

name: variational approximation of a posterior
essential_semantics: Optimisation over a family of distributions minimising a divergence, with the family and divergence direction stated.
canonical_example: minimise KL(q || p) over mean-field Gaussian q
rationale: Optimising over distributions is optimisation whose decision variable is a measure, a demanding composition.

name: identifiability of parameters
essential_semantics: Distinct parameter values induce distinct distributions; failure means the data cannot distinguish them.
canonical_example: in y = (a + b) x only a + b is identified
rationale: It is a quantified structural claim about a model, and an unidentified model produces confident nonsense.

name: missingness mechanism
essential_semantics: MCAR, MAR and MNAR as distinct conditional-independence assumptions about the missingness indicator.
canonical_example: missingness independent of the unobserved value given covariates (MAR)
rationale: The mechanism determines whether analysis is valid; it is an assumption that must be stated to be criticised.

name: sampling and experimental design
essential_semantics: How units were selected or assigned (randomisation, stratification, clustering, blocking), which determines valid inference.
canonical_example: stratified sample with unequal inclusion probabilities
rationale: Design is the bridge between data and population; analysis ignoring design is systematically biased.

name: intervention (do-operator) distinct from conditioning
essential_semantics: P(Y | do(X = x)) is not P(Y | X = x); intervention modifies the generating mechanism.
canonical_example: P(recovery | do(treatment)) versus P(recovery | treatment)
rationale: The conditioning/intervention distinction is the central formal content of causal inference and is invisible in ordinary probability notation.

name: counterfactual quantities
essential_semantics: Potential outcomes Y(1), Y(0) for the same unit, only one of which is observed.
canonical_example: the individual treatment effect Y_i(1) - Y_i(0)
rationale: Counterfactuals are not expressible in the observational joint distribution alone; representing them requires extra structure.

name: confounding and adjustment sets
essential_semantics: Which variables must be conditioned on for a causal estimand to be identified, derived from an assumed causal structure.
canonical_example: adjusting for Z blocks the backdoor path X <- Z -> Y
rationale: Adjustment validity is a graph-theoretic property of the assumed model, not a property of the data.

name: time-indexed dependent data
essential_semantics: Observations with a temporal order and dependence, with stationarity assumptions explicit.
canonical_example: AR(1): y_t = phi y_{t-1} + eps_t
rationale: Independence-based inference fails here; the dependence assumption must be part of the model representation.

name: descriptive summaries with defined conventions
essential_semantics: Mean, median, quantiles, variance of a sample with denominator and interpolation conventions explicit and with population analogues distinguished.
canonical_example: sample variance with denominator n-1
rationale: Convention differences (n versus n-1, quantile interpolation) change reported numbers and are almost never recorded.
